verses.text: Be imitators of me, even as I also am of Christ.
Now I praise you, brothers, that you remember me in all things, and hold firm the traditions, even as I delivered them to you.
But I would have you know that the head  of every man is Christ, and the head  of the woman is man, and the head  of Christ is God.
Every man praying or prophesying, having his head covered, dishonors his head.
But every woman praying or prophesying with her head uncovered dishonors her head. For it is one and the same thing as if she were shaved.
For if a woman is not covered, let her hair also be cut off. But if it is shameful for a woman to have her hair cut off or be shaved, let her be covered.
For a man indeed ought not to have his head covered, because he is the image and glory of God, but the woman is the glory of the man.
For man is not from woman, but woman from man;
for man wasn’t created for the woman, but woman for the man.
For this cause the woman ought to have authority over her own head, because of the angels.
Nevertheless, neither is the woman independent of the man, nor the man independent of the woman, in the Lord.
For as woman came from man, so a man also comes through a woman; but all things are from God.
Judge for yourselves. Is it appropriate that a woman pray to God unveiled?
Doesn’t even nature itself teach you that if a man has long hair, it is a dishonor to him?
But if a woman has long hair, it is a glory to her, for her hair is given to her for a covering.
But if any man seems to be contentious, we have no such custom, neither do God’s assemblies.
But in giving you this command, I don’t praise you, that you come together not for the better but for the worse.
For first of all, when you come together in the assembly, I hear that divisions exist among you, and I partly believe it.
For there also must be factions among you, that those who are approved may be revealed among you.
When therefore you assemble yourselves together, it is not the Lord’s supper that you eat.
For in your eating each one takes his own supper first. One is hungry, and another is drunken.
What, don’t you have houses to eat and to drink in? Or do you despise God’s assembly, and put them to shame who don’t have? What shall I tell you? Shall I praise you? In this I don’t praise you.
For I received from the Lord that which also I delivered to you, that the Lord Jesus on the night in which he was betrayed took bread.
When he had given thanks, he broke it, and said, “Take, eat. This is my body, which is broken for you. Do this in memory of me.”
In the same way he also took the cup, after supper, saying, “This cup is the new covenant in my blood. Do this, as often as you drink, in memory of me.”
For as often as you eat this bread and drink this cup, you proclaim the Lord’s death until he comes.
Therefore whoever eats this bread or drinks the Lord’s cup in a way unworthy of the Lord will be guilty of the body and the blood of the Lord.
But let a man examine himself, and so let him eat of the bread, and drink of the cup.
For he who eats and drinks in an unworthy way eats and drinks judgment to himself, if he doesn’t discern the Lord’s body.
For this cause many among you are weak and sickly, and not a few sleep.
For if we discerned ourselves, we wouldn’t be judged.
But when we are judged, we are punished by the Lord, that we may not be condemned with the world.
Therefore, my brothers, when you come together to eat, wait for one another.
But if anyone is hungry, let him eat at home, lest your coming together be for judgment. The rest I will set in order whenever I come.

footnotes.content: Paul gives us the boldest chain: imitate me as I imitate Christ. Not 'be perfect like me,' but 'follow the direction I'm walking.' That's the invitation—to step into the same path he's taken, with all its stumbling and grace.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Paul sees them holding firm to the traditions he passed on. In a world bent on forgetting what we've been given, there's something steady in a people who remember. He's encouraging that faithfulness—the willingness to steward what has been entrusted.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A chain of headship: Christ over man, man over woman, God over Christ. This speaks of authority as responsibility, not domination. Each link depends on the one above it—Christ serves the Father, man serves as Christ would, woman responds to sacrificial leadership. It's less about rank than rhythm.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A man with his head covered in worship clouds the image—his authority to lead in prayer comes from reflecting Christ's headship. To cover the head is to obscure that likeness. The practice meant something specific in that moment, in that place.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A woman uncovered shames her covering—Paul connects her head to the authority she's meant to reflect. The veil wasn't mere fashion; it was a sign. To pray unveiled was to step out of that visible sign of order. I think he's asking: don't abandon the very sign that names your dignity.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: If uncovering means shame, then be covered. Paul's logic is bracing—don't pretend indifference costs nothing. A shorn head was public disgrace in that culture. So either wear the covering that marks your place, or face the public mark of having refused it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A man is the image and glory of God; a woman is the glory of man. Not lesser—different in the order. She reflects his reflected glory, just as he reflects God's. There's no distance here that dishonors her—she is woven into the chain of reflection itself.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Woman came from man's rib—Genesis echoes here. Paul anchors his teaching in creation itself. She was drawn from him, bone of his bone. The order comes from the very making of her, not from some rule imposed later.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Man wasn't made for the woman; woman for the man. Purpose shapes the relationship. She was created as a helper, as one who completes what he alone cannot do. This isn't diminishment—it's the deepest kind of interdependence.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A woman ought to have authority over her own head because of the angels. A strange phrase—'because of the angels'—but I think Paul is saying her covering is a sign visible even to the heavenly watchers. There's something sacred in the order itself, something the powers recognize.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Yet neither is independent of the other in the Lord. Just when we might think the order absolute, Paul catches himself: we need each other. In Christ, neither stands alone. The covering speaks of order, but the gospel speaks of mutual need. Both are true.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Woman came from man, yes—but now man comes through woman. Every man is born of a woman. The circle completes itself. And all things—both the making and the bearing—come from God. No one stands apart from this web of God's design.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Is it appropriate for a woman to pray unveiled? Paul appeals to their own judgment. He's not bullying them into obedience—he's inviting them to see what's fitting. Sometimes wisdom means helping people notice what they already know in their bones.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Nature itself teaches that long hair on a man is a dishonor. He appeals to what is written in creation—the way things are made. I don't think he's speaking of absolute nature, but of the nature as it was understood in his time and place. Context speaks.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A woman's long hair is her glory—given to her for a covering. Here's the mercy in it: she has her own glory, her own adornment. The hair itself is a natural sign of the very covering Paul has been discussing. The body speaks what words can sometimes obscure.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: If someone wants to be contentious about this, Paul says gently: we have no such custom, nor do God's assemblies elsewhere. He's not legislating forever—he's describing what the churches do. Don't let stubbornness eclipse the peace of shared practice.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Paul shifts gear sharply: when you gather, you don't come together for the better but the worse. It's a damning summary. What should be the church's highest moment—eating together as Christ's body—has become a scandal of division. His praise stops here.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Divisions exist among you—he's heard the reports. The church is splintering. Rich and poor, one group against another. Paul doesn't dismiss the rumors; he partly believes them because he knows how easily the flesh wins when we're not watching Christ together.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Factions must be among you, so that the approved may be revealed. Paul isn't excusing division—he's saying that in the furnace of conflict, character shows itself. Those who lean into Jesus become visible. Those who drift away show their true direction too.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: When you assemble, it's not the Lord's supper you eat. Ouch. They're eating together, yes, but not eating His supper. The form remains; the substance is gone. You can gather as a congregation and still miss the central act of remembering Christ's death.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Each takes his own supper first. One goes hungry, another is drunk. The scandal is plain: they're eating the meal meant to unite them as a monument to Christ's self-giving, yet they're using it to show who has and who hasn't. No wonder Christ's presence is absent.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Don't you have houses to eat in? Why shame the poor by feasting while they starve? Paul's sarcasm burns. The rich could eat at home; the church meal was meant for the poor to share. To turn it into a display of wealth in the gathering itself is to mock the very body of Christ.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: I received from the Lord what I also delivered to you. The night He was betrayed, He took bread. Paul anchors the Lord's Supper in that singular night—the very moment Christ's body was about to be broken. This isn't custom we've smoothed down; it's a transaction of love in the shadow of the cross.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Take, eat. This is my body, broken for you. The words are stark. His body is given—not symbolically, but really given up. 'Do this in memory of me.' Every time we eat, we remember the breaking. We place ourselves under the sign of His sacrifice.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: This cup is the new covenant in my blood. With every sip, we're tasting the sealing of a new bond between God and His people. The old covenants required blood; this one too, but His blood—poured out to make us His forever. 'Do this in memory of me.'
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: As often as you eat and drink, you proclaim His death until He comes. The Supper isn't nostalgia—it's announcement. Every time, we're saying aloud to the heavens: He died for us. We're speaking the gospel with our mouths and our hunger. We'll keep doing it until He returns.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Whoever eats unworthily is guilty of the body and blood. This is weight Paul won't let us ignore. To eat without reverence, without remembering whose death we're eating, is to condemn ourselves. The meal we come to for grace becomes a snare if we come carelessly.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Let a man examine himself before eating the bread and drinking the cup. A pause before the table. Look at your heart. Are you chasing mercy or just habit? The examination isn't punishment—it's the way we ready ourselves to receive what's being offered.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He who eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment. Not because God is harsh, but because we're eating a covenant meal while blind to what the covenant cost. To participate in Christ's death without feeling the weight of it is to eat our own condemnation.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Many among you are weak, sickly, and sleep. Paul sees the connection—their careless eating has consequences. God disciplines the ones He loves. These aren't punishments so much as wakeup calls. Something is wrong between them and the Lord, and their bodies are showing it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: If we discerned ourselves, we wouldn't be judged. Self-examination is preventive grace. We could catch ourselves, turn back, make things right before God has to step in and shake us. The offer is standing: look at your own heart now, while there's still room to repent.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: When judged, we're punished by the Lord so we won't be condemned with the world. His discipline is mercy wearing a stern face. He's not casting us out; He's keeping us close enough to hurt us rather than lose us. To be pruned is to remain in the vine.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: When you gather to eat, wait for one another. The meal means nothing if only half the body is fed. There's a rhythm here: we slow down, we look around, we see who's missing. The Supper teaches us to eat as one, not as competitors.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: If hungry, eat at home—don't make the church meal about filling your belly. Readers today hear an echo of this: when we gather, we're not meeting our own hunger first. We're gathering to remember Christ together. The real feast is remembrance, not bread.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
